units.name: flask-app
units.role: The application object at the center of a Flask program: routing, dispatch, error handling, WSGI entrypoint.
units.description: This is the heart of the Flask web framework: the 'App' object a developer creates to build a website or API. One file (sansio/app.py) defines the general shape of what an application object can do -- hold configuration, register URL routes, keep track of error handlers and blueprints, build a Jinja templating environment. The other file (app.py) fills in the concrete, real-world behavior: it makes the object callable as a standard web server application, matches incoming requests to the right route, catches and formats errors, runs the built-in development web server, and turns whatever a view function returns into a proper HTTP response. It must never silently swallow an unhandled exception without logging it, and it must never treat two different registered URL rules as interchangeable.

units.name: scaffold
units.role: The shared decorator vocabulary both an App and a Blueprint use to describe their routes and hooks.
units.description: This defines the common toolbox that both a Flask application and a Flask blueprint use to describe themselves: the route/get/post decorators, before-request/after-request/teardown hooks, error-handler registration, template filter/global/test registration, and the logic for locating a component's static and template folders on disk. Neither the App nor the Blueprint reimplements this; they both build on it, so a decorator written once behaves the same whether it's attached to the whole app or to one blueprint. It must never register a rule after the app has already finished starting up.

units.name: blueprints
units.role: A deferred, composable group of routes/handlers that gets replayed onto a real app later.
units.description: This is Flask's Blueprint feature: a way to package up a group of routes, view functions, error handlers, and template helpers so they can be defined once -- often in a separate file or a reusable plugin -- and attached to a real running application later, possibly under a URL prefix, possibly more than once. A Blueprint just records what a developer configures on it; when the application registers it, those recorded instructions are replayed onto the real app so the routes become live. It must never register itself directly as if it were the running application.

entrypoints.name: Blueprint

entrypoints.name: Blueprint.register

units.name: context
units.role: Tracks 'which app and which request are active right now' and notifies listeners of lifecycle transitions.
units.description: This is the plumbing that keeps track of which application and which web request are being handled right now, as code runs. When Flask starts handling a request (or a CLI command, or a test), it pushes a small context object remembering the current app, the incoming request, and a per-request scratch space. Other code anywhere in the program can then just say 'give me the current app' or 'give me the current request' without passing those objects around explicitly, and each concurrent request gets its own isolated copy. When a context is pushed or torn down, this unit also rings a small set of internal bells (signals) so other parts of Flask, or a developer's own code, can react to 'a request just started' or 'the app context just ended'. It must never let one request's data leak into a concurrently running request.

units.name: wrappers
units.role: Flask's own Request and Response classes: what an incoming request and an outgoing response look like.
units.description: This defines Flask's own versions of the 'Request' and 'Response' objects -- the two objects that represent, respectively, an incoming web request and the reply Flask sends back. They build on a lower-level toolkit's request/response objects but add Flask-specific conveniences: knowing which blueprint the current request belongs to, honoring the app's configured content-size and cookie-size limits, and using Flask's own JSON handling. Every request a browser sends to a Flask app, and every response the app sends back, is represented by one of these two classes by default. It must never expose one request's data through a different, concurrently handled request's object.

entrypoints.name: Request
entrypoints.plain: Represents one incoming HTTP request, with Flask-specific extras like JSON body access.

entrypoints.name: Response
entrypoints.plain: Represents the HTTP response Flask is going to send back.

units.name: json
units.role: Turns Python values into JSON text and back, for HTTP responses and for signed session cookies.
units.description: This is Flask's toolkit for turning ordinary Python values -- dicts, lists, numbers, dates, IDs -- into JSON text and back again. It powers two everyday things: converting data a view returns into a proper JSON HTTP response, and safely packing session data into the signed cookie Flask sends to a browser, including types plain JSON can't normally hold, like dates, UUIDs, and raw bytes. It must never lose information when round-tripping a value it explicitly claims to support (a datetime that comes back out must equal the one that went in).

entrypoints.name: jsonify

entrypoints.name: dumps

effects.description: dump()/load() write to or read from a file-like object the caller supplies; this unit never opens a file itself.

units.name: sessions
units.role: Remembers a visitor's data between requests by storing it in a signed browser cookie.
units.description: This is how Flask remembers information about a visitor between separate web requests -- their 'session' -- such as being logged in. It stores that information inside a browser cookie rather than on the server, but protects it from tampering by cryptographically signing the cookie's contents with the app's secret key. It also defines the general contract any session storage strategy must follow, so the default cookie-based approach could be swapped for something else, like a server-side database, without changing the rest of the framework. It must never accept a session cookie whose signature doesn't match, and must never store the session in a way a browser or attacker could silently edit undetected.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface
entrypoints.plain: The contract any session storage strategy must implement.

entrypoints.name: SecureCookieSessionInterface
entrypoints.plain: The default session storage: a signed cookie.

entrypoints.name: SessionMixin

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.save_session
entrypoints.plain: Writes the session data onto the outgoing response as a cookie.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.make_null_session

effects.description: Reads the session cookie off the incoming request and writes/deletes it on the outgoing response.
Signs and verifies cookie contents using itsdangerous (HMAC-based signing).

units.name: config
units.role: Loads app settings from Python files, other files, environment variables, or plain objects into one dict-like object.
units.description: This is Flask's configuration system: a dictionary-like object holding all the settings for an app, such as its secret key or whether debug mode is on. It offers convenience methods for loading those settings from the different places a real project might keep them: a Python file, an object or module with uppercase attributes, a JSON/TOML/etc. file via a caller-supplied loader, environment variables, or a plain dictionary. It must never silently ignore a config source a developer explicitly asked it to load.

entrypoints.name: Config
entrypoints.plain: The dict-like object holding an app's settings, with methods to load them from various sources.

entrypoints.name: ConfigAttribute
entrypoints.plain: Exposes one config key as a normal attribute on the app object, e.g. app.secret_key.

effects.description: from_pyfile() and from_file() open() a file path joined with the app's root path to read configuration data.
from_pyfile() compiles and executes the contents of the opened file as Python code.
from_envvar() reads an environment variable to find a config file path; from_prefixed_env() reads every FLASK_-prefixed environment variable.
from_prefixed_env() and from_file() deserialize string/file content into richer Python types via json.loads or a caller-supplied loader.

units.name: templating
units.role: Wires the Jinja2 template engine into Flask, merging an app's and its blueprints' template folders.
units.description: This is the glue that lets a Flask app render HTML (or other text) templates using the Jinja2 templating engine. It defines a custom Jinja environment that knows about Flask apps, and a loader that automatically searches the main app's template folder as well as every registered blueprint's template folder when looking up a template by name. It also provides the functions a developer calls to produce output -- render a named template, render a template given as a string, and streaming versions of both -- announcing 'before render' and 'rendered' events other parts of Flask can listen to. It must never render a template using stale variables left over from a previous request.

entrypoints.name: Environment
entrypoints.plain: Flask's customized Jinja2 environment, aware of the app it belongs to.

entrypoints.name: DispatchingJinjaLoader
entrypoints.plain: A template loader that searches the app's and every blueprint's template folder.

Sends before_render_template and template_rendered signals around each render.

units.name: helpers
units.role: The everyday vocabulary of things a view does: build a URL, redirect, abort, flash a message, send a file.
units.description: This is Flask's toolbox of small convenience functions used while handling a web request: building a URL for a named route, sending the browser to another page, stopping a request early with an HTTP error, queuing a one-time notice for the next page load, turning a view function's return value into a proper response, streaming a response while keeping request data available, and serving a file or a folder's file as a download. It also has a few lower-level utilities used by Flask's own internals: reading environment variables for debug/.env behavior and figuring out where an app's code lives on disk. It must never build a URL for a route that doesn't exist without raising an error.

entrypoints.name: get_load_dotenv

entrypoints.name: stream_with_context

units.name: cli
units.role: The `flask` command line program: discover the app, run the dev server, open a shell, list routes.
units.description: This is the `flask` command line program. It figures out which Flask app to run -- from a flag, an environment variable, a factory function, or a wsgi.py/app.py file -- then offers commands to start the built-in development web server, drop into an interactive Python shell pre-loaded with the app, or list all registered URL routes. It also loads settings from .env/.flaskenv files before anything else runs. It must never start the development server bound to a network interface the developer didn't ask for.

entrypoints.name: main
entrypoints.plain: The `flask` command line program's entrypoint.

entrypoints.name: ScriptInfo
entrypoints.plain: Lazily locates and loads the Flask app a CLI command should operate on.

entrypoints.name: AppGroup
entrypoints.plain: A group of CLI commands attached to an app or blueprint (e.g. `flask db ...`).

entrypoints.name: load_dotenv
entrypoints.plain: Loads variables from .env/.flaskenv files into the environment.

entrypoints.name: show_server_banner
entrypoints.plain: Prints the startup banner (debug mode, environment) when the dev server launches.

Launches an interactive Python REPL for `flask shell`, and dynamically imports plugin commands and the user's application module by string.

units.name: testing
units.role: Simulates HTTP requests and CLI invocations against a Flask app, without a real server.
units.description: This provides Flask's built-in toolkit for writing automated tests. It lets a developer send fake web requests into an app and inspect the responses without starting a real web server or opening a network socket, and lets them invoke the app's command-line commands in a sandboxed way. It is the machinery behind `app.test_client()` and `app.test_cli_runner()`. It must never make a real network connection while simulating a request.

entrypoints.name: FlaskClient
entrypoints.plain: Sends simulated HTTP requests into an app and returns the responses.

entrypoints.name: FlaskCliRunner
entrypoints.plain: Invokes the app's CLI commands in a sandboxed way for testing.

entrypoints.name: EnvironBuilder
entrypoints.plain: Builds the request environment used to simulate an incoming request.

effects.description: Reads the installed werkzeug package's version via package metadata to build a default User-Agent header.
Drives simulated requests through the WSGI app in-process; explicitly not a real network connection.

units.name: views
units.role: Class-based views: an alternative to writing one function per route.
units.description: This gives developers a second way to write the code that handles a web request: instead of one function per URL, a class. `View` is the base class a developer subclasses and registers with a route; `MethodView` automatically routes GET/POST/PUT/etc. requests to correspondingly named methods on the class, handy for REST-style APIs. It is part of the framework's public toolkit that application code imports and uses directly -- it is not called by any other part of Flask itself. It must never dispatch a request to a method the class doesn't actually define for that HTTP verb.

entrypoints.name: View
entrypoints.plain: Base class for writing a route's handler as a class instead of a function.

entrypoints.name: View.as_view
entrypoints.plain: Turns a View subclass into a view function that can be registered with add_url_rule.

entrypoints.name: MethodView
entrypoints.plain: A View that dispatches to a same-named method per HTTP verb (get/post/put/...).

units.name: debughelpers
units.role: Friendly, extra-detailed error messages for common developer mistakes, shown only in debug mode.
units.description: This provides friendly, extra-detailed error messages that only show up when a Flask app is running in debug mode. When a developer forgets to set the right form encoding, submits a redirect that would silently drop form data, or Flask can't find a template file, these helpers explain exactly what went wrong instead of showing a generic, confusing error. It must never change the app's actual behavior -- only the clarity of the diagnostic shown when something looks like a developer mistake.

entrypoints.name: attach_enctype_error_multidict

entrypoints.name: explain_template_loading_attempts

entrypoints.name: DebugFilesKeyError
entrypoints.plain: A more helpful error raised when a form file field is missing due to a form/enctype mistake.

effects.description: Logs a multi-line diagnostic report of template-loader lookup attempts through the app's logger.

units.name: logging
units.role: Sets up the app's default logger, so app.logger works without configuration.
units.description: This provides Flask's built-in error/debug logger. When a Flask app first accesses its `logger`, this creates or reuses a standard logger named after the app, turns on debug-level logging automatically in debug mode, and, if the developer hasn't set up their own logging handler, attaches a sensible default one that prints nicely formatted messages to the web server's error stream. It must never attach a duplicate default handler on repeated access.

entrypoints.name: create_logger
entrypoints.plain: Creates or reuses the app's logger, configuring a sensible default handler.

entrypoints.name: wsgi_errors_stream

wsgi_errors_stream writes to the active request's wsgi.errors stream, or to stderr outside of a request.

units.name: typing
units.role: The shared vocabulary describing what a route handler, error handler, or template callback must look like.
units.description: This is Flask's shared dictionary of 'shapes' -- it describes, for developer tooling, what a piece of code must look like to be usable as a route handler, an error handler, a before/after-request hook, or a template filter. It contains no logic that runs; it exists so other parts of Flask, and a developer's own editor or type checker, share one vocabulary for these callback shapes instead of everyone redefining them. It must never describe a shape that doesn't match what the code accepting that callback actually calls it with.

units.name: package-api
units.role: The public `flask` namespace: re-exports the building blocks from every other unit under one import.
units.description: This is the single file a developer's `import flask` or `from flask import Flask, request` actually reaches. It has no logic of its own -- it just gathers together the pieces built by every other unit (the App class, the request/session proxies, the JSON helpers, the templating functions, and so on) so a developer never has to know or care which internal file any of them actually live in. It must never re-export a name whose real definition it doesn't already depend on.

violations_observed.note: Flask.test_client lazily imports FlaskClient by name (`from .testing import FlaskClient as cls`) rather than the testing unit exposing a factory; a benign, deliberate lazy-import pattern to avoid a hard import cycle, not a real internals violation.

DispatchingJinjaLoader reads app.config['EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING'] directly as a dict key rather than through a named App method; config access here is genuinely ad hoc rather than going through a declared entrypoint.

AppContext push calls app.session_interface.open_session(...)/make_null_session(...) through an instance attribute of type SessionInterface rather than a module-level entrypoint; the sessions unit's contract methods are reached indirectly via the app object, not called directly.
